q: What marks the END of the embryo stage?
o: A crown–rump length of about 3 cm
e: The end of the embryo stage is a size criterion, not a date — about 3 cm crown–rump.

q: About how much amniotic fluid is present at term?
e: Amniotic fluid is about 1 L at term, constantly absorbed and replenished; it allows fetal movement, protects, and aids thermoregulation.

q: Fetal lung fluid is best described as:
o: Low pH, low protein and bicarbonate, high sodium and chloride
High pH, high protein, low sodium
Identical in composition to amniotic fluid
e: The fetal lung secretes its own fluid — low pH, low protein and bicarbonate, high Na⁺ and Cl⁻ — keeping developing airways patent and shaping air spaces.

q: What is the main function of fetal lung fluid?
o: Maintains airway patency and shapes the developing air spaces
Supplies oxygen to the fetal alveoli
e: Fetal lung fluid keeps developing airways patent and shapes the formation, size and shape of potential air spaces.

q: Which is NOT one of the amniotic-fluid lung-maturity tests listed on the slides?
e: The five lung-maturity tests are L/S ratio, shake/foam test, SAR, TDx-FLM, and fluorescence polarization. Apgar is a newborn score.

q: The pseudoglandular stage of lung development spans:
e: Embryonal = first 7 weeks (lungs begin at 24 days); pseudoglandular = 7–16 weeks, when the lungs begin to look like glands.

q: Lung development begins at about what point?
e: In the embryonal stage (first 7 weeks), the lungs begin to develop at about 24 days.

q: Low birth weight is defined as a birth weight below:
e: Low birth weight = < 2500 g, a weight-only label. SGA (< 10th percentile) is the GA-adjusted label. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Under current week bands, "full term" is:
e: Early term 37–38 6/7, full term 39–40 6/7, late term 41–41 6/7, post-term ≥ 42 wk. The single "37–42 wk" label was retired in 2013. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: A late-preterm infant is born at:
e: Preterm is < 37 0/7 weeks; late preterm is 34 0/7 – 36 6/7. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: A two-vessel cord (single umbilical artery) is significant because it:
o: Is a marker for congenital anomalies
Means the umbilical vein is absent
Is the normal finding in preterm infants
e: One artery + one vein (~0.5–1% of pregnancies) is associated with cardiac, renal/GU, GI and skeletal anomalies and trisomy 18/13. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: On X-ray, where should a high UAC tip sit?
e: High UAC = T6–T9 (preferred); low = L3–L5; avoid T10–L2 (celiac/SMA/renal). (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Where should a UVC tip sit on X-ray?
o: At the IVC/right-atrium junction, about T8–T9
e: A UVC travels straight up; its tip belongs at the IVC–right atrium junction, ~T8–T9. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Why is the umbilical cord clamped rather than tied?
o: Wharton's jelly makes the cord slippery and compressible
The cord has no blood vessels
Clamping speeds up delivery of the placenta
e: Wharton's jelly makes the cord slippery and compressible, so it is clamped. Lean jelly is linked to growth restriction; excess jelly to gestational diabetes and hydrops. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Wharton's jelly is made mainly of:
e: It is mucoid connective tissue — mostly hyaluronic acid plus chondroitin sulfate, which hold water to make a gel. Not fat, not muscle. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: How is fundal height measured?
o: Symphysis pubis to the top of the fundus, with a tape measure
Width of the maternal abdomen at the umbilicus
e: Fundal height = tape-measure distance from the symphysis pubis to the top of the fundus.

q: What does the contraction stress test detect?
e: The contraction stress test detects uteroplacental insufficiency.

q: Which is NOT a method of obtaining the fetal heart rate?
o: Pulse oximeter on the maternal finger
Spiral electrode on the fetal scalp
e: FHR is obtained by auscultation, external abdominal transducer, abdominal electrodes, or a fetal scalp spiral electrode.

q: Which is one of the five components of parturition?
e: Parturition: cervical dilation, rupture of membranes, uterine contraction, separation of the placenta, and shrinking of the uterus.

q: On a cervical exam, station 0 means the presenting part is:
e: Station runs −5 to +5 relative to the ischial spines; 0 = engaged, +5 = crowning. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: What does 48 hours of tocolysis actually buy?
o: Time for antenatal steroids and maternal transport
Time for the cervix to close permanently
e: Tocolytics don't stop preterm birth by themselves; the 48 h allow antenatal corticosteroids, transport to a NICU center, and MgSO₄ neuroprotection. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: What is the betamethasone regimen for fetal lung maturation?
e: Betamethasone 12 mg IM × 2, 24 h apart (dexamethasone 6 mg IM × 4, q12h), recommended at 24 0/7–33 6/7 weeks. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Antenatal corticosteroids reduce neonatal RDS by:
o: Accelerating type II pneumocyte maturation and surfactant production
e: They speed type II cell maturation and surfactant production, reducing RDS, IVH, NEC and mortality. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Painful, dark-red bleeding with a rigid, board-like uterus suggests:
e: Abruption is painful with a firm, tender uterus and often a nonreassuring FHR. Previa is painless, bright red, with a soft uterus. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Why is a digital vaginal exam contraindicated in placenta previa?
o: It can disrupt the placenta over the os and cause catastrophic hemorrhage
It causes premature rupture of membranes
It spreads infection to the fetus
e: In third-trimester painless bleeding: ultrasound first, hands off the cervix. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: A fetal scalp pH of 7.22 calls for:
e: ≥ 7.25 normal; 7.21–7.24 pre-acidosis → repeat within 30 min; ≤ 7.20 acidosis → deliver immediately. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Which umbilical cord sample has the LOWER pH?
o: The artery, which reflects the fetus
The vein, which reflects the placenta
It depends on the mode of delivery
e: Artery mean pH 7.24–7.27; vein 7.32–7.34. If the two match, you probably sampled the vein twice. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Why do babies born by elective cesarean before labor get TTN?
o: They miss the labor catecholamine surge that switches the lung to fluid absorption
Their surfactant is destroyed by anesthesia
e: Labor catecholamines and glucocorticoids activate ENaC, moving Na⁺ and water out of the alveoli. Without labor, fetal lung fluid is retained. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Without a medical indication, an elective cesarean should not be done before:
e: Elective (no-labor) cesareans carry the highest TTN risk, so ACOG says not before 39 0/7 weeks. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: A single maternal temperature of what is enough to diagnose chorioamnionitis?
e: ≥ 39.0 °C once is enough. At 38.0–38.9 °C you need two readings plus one other sign (fetal HR > 160, WBC > 15,000, purulent fluid). (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: ACOG's preferred term for chorioamnionitis is:
e: Since 2017 ACOG prefers "intraamniotic infection"; "Triple I" is the NICHD research label. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Where do you look to judge a newborn's color during resuscitation?
e: Visually inspect the central trunk, then confirm with a pulse oximeter and give O₂ if needed.

q: During PPV, the HR is 80. Per the slide, what next?
o: Continue PPV and monitor oxygen saturation
e: If HR is > 60 but < 100, continue PPV, monitor SpO₂, and evaluate chest rise.

q: Which is an intubation difficulty named on the slides?
o: Tube too short to reach the larynx
Damage to the vocal cords from suction
e: Named difficulties: hard to visualize landmarks, esophageal insertion, and advancing too far down the trachea.

q: What is the target preductal SpO₂ at 5 minutes after birth (NRP 9th ed.)?
e: 2 min 65–70 · 3 min 70–75 · 4 min 75–80 · 5 min 80–85 · 10 min 85–95%. The 1-min row was removed in the 9th edition. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: What is the target preductal SpO₂ at 10 minutes after birth?
e: NRP 9th edition: 10 min = 85–95%, measured on the right hand/wrist. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: What ETT size does a 3.0 kg term newborn need?
e: ≤ 1200 g → 2.5 · 1201–2200 g → 3.0 · > 2200 g → 3.5 mm ID. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: A 1,000 g (26-week) infant needs what ETT size?
e: Infants ≤ 1200 g (< 28 weeks) get a 2.5 mm tube. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Using the "6 + weight" rule, how deep at the lip is the ETT for a 3 kg newborn?
e: Neonatal depth at the upper lip (cm) = 6 + weight in kg → 6 + 3 = 9 cm. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: After 60 s of compressions the newborn's HR is still below 60. Next step?
e: HR < 100 → PPV; < 60 after 30 s of good PPV → compressions 3:1 with 100% O₂; still < 60 after 60 s → epinephrine. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Which is NOT one of the 7 physical criteria in gestational-age exams?
e: The seven: vernix, skin maturity, lanugo, ear recoil, breast tissue, genitalia, sole creases.

q: How many criteria does the New Ballard Score use?
e: New Ballard: 12 criteria, total −10 to +50, best at 12–24 h; every 5 points = 2 weeks. Dubowitz uses 21. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: A New Ballard score of 40 corresponds to what gestational age?
e: Every 5 points = 2 weeks, so a score of 40 = 40 weeks. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Which is one of the 7 newborn observation findings on the slide?
e: The checklist: tachypnea, tachycardia, grunting, retractions, inability to maintain temperature, reduced vigor, limp appearance. No thresholds are given.

q: Which neonatal reflexes are listed on the slide?
e: The four: rooting, suck, grasp, Moro. The neurologic exam depends on intrauterine development.

q: Which is one of the three stated purposes of the neonatal physical exam?
o: Determining successful transition to extrauterine life
e: Purposes: discover physical defects, confirm successful transition to extrauterine life, maintain thermoregulation.

q: In the Quiet Examination, what do you observe?
o: Color, lanugo, activity, overall look and respiration
e: Quiet exam = observe color, lanugo, activity, overall look, respiration — before any hands-on exam.

q: Which comes FIRST in the Ch05 neonatal exam sequence?
e: Anatomic background → observation survey → history + GA → size → quiet exam → hands-on → neurologic exam.

q: Which does neonatal pulmonary function testing measure?
o: Compliance, resistance, FRC and crying vital capacity
Peak expiratory flow by forced effort
e: Neonatal PFT measures compliance and resistance, WOB, expiratory flows, lung volumes, FRC, crying vital capacity.

q: For neonatal PFT, sedation may cause untoward events in which condition?
e: Sedation risk: central hypoventilation, CNS depression, OSA, severe obesity, esophagitis/gastritis, hepatic or renal dysfunction.

q: What separates benign acrocyanosis from central cyanosis?
o: Trunk, tongue and mucous membranes stay pink with normal SpO₂
e: Acrocyanosis is normal for 24–48 h; treat with warmth, not oxygen. Central cyanosis beyond ~10 min of life is never acrocyanosis. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Why can a severely anemic hypoxemic patient look pink?
o: Cyanosis needs ~5 g/dL desaturated Hb, which anemia rarely reaches
Low Hb makes oximetry read low
e: Cyanosis depends on the absolute amount of reduced Hb, so it appears late or never in anemia and early in polycythemia. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: At roughly what SpO₂ does cyanosis become visible?
e: SpO₂ ~80–85% (PaO₂ ~35–50 mm Hg). Cyanosis is a late, unreliable sign — use the pulse oximeter. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: How do the slides define thermoregulation?
o: Equality between heat dissipation and heat production
e: "The maintenance of equality between heat dissipation and heat production by the body" — one of the most important parts of neonatal care.

q: The internal thermal gradient is the temperature difference between:
o: The warm body core and the cooler skin
e: Internal gradient = core to skin; regulated by metabolic rate, subcutaneous fat, surface area, and core-to-skin distance.

q: Which is NOT a regulator of the internal thermal gradient?
o: Distance from body core to skin
e: The four: metabolic rate, subcutaneous fat, surface area for heat loss, and core-to-skin distance.

q: Physiologic jaundice in a term infant typically peaks on:
e: Physiologic jaundice starts after 24 h, peaks day 3–5, resolves by 2–3 weeks. Jaundice in the first 24 h is never physiologic. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Breast-milk jaundice (vs breastfeeding jaundice) is characterized by:
o: Late onset in a baby who is feeding well and thriving
First-week onset in a dehydrated baby
e: Breastfeeding jaundice: early, too little milk, baby doing poorly. Breast-milk jaundice: later (peaks week 2), milk inhibits conjugation, baby fine. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: How does phototherapy clear bilirubin?
o: Blue-green light converts it to water-soluble lumirubin
It conjugates bilirubin in the liver
e: 460–490 nm light photoisomerizes unconjugated bilirubin to lumirubin, excreted in bile and urine without conjugation. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Which blood-group incompatibility can affect a firstborn?
o: ABO (mother type O, infant A or B)
e: ABO uses preformed maternal IgG, so it can affect the firstborn and is usually mild. Rh needs prior sensitization, so usually the second pregnancy. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Per the slide, direct bilirubin above what is pathologic?
e: Answer the slide column: direct bilirubin > 1.5 mg/dL. Current teaching uses ≥ 5 mg/dL or > 20% of total.

q: Which is a consequence of asphyxia listed on Ch07 S18?
e: HIE, periventricular leukomalacia, bowel ischemia, NEC, and DIC.

q: Which is an RDS treatment listed on the slides?
o: Glucocorticoids given to the mother before delivery
e: Ch07 S4: prevention, maternal glucocorticoids, artificial surfactant replacement, and ventilation that doesn't damage the lungs.

q: ROP Stage 2 is defined by:
o: A ridge rising from the plane of the retina
e: Stage 1 = thin white demarcation line; Stage 2 = a ridge rising from the retina, with new vessels possibly behind it.

q: Which is the only cause-and-effect ROP statement on the slide?
o: Vasoconstriction leads to necrosis of the vessels
e: ROP: scar behind the lens, linked to oxygen use, immature capillaries, and vasoconstriction → vessel necrosis.

q: Rank newborn respiratory distress at term, most common first:
e: TTN → RDS → MAS → pneumonia/sepsis → pneumothorax, CHD, CDH. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Which chest film clears within 24–72 hours?
e: TTN: mildly increased volume, perihilar streaks, fissure fluid — clearing in 24–72 h is the clincher. RDS has low volume and ground glass; MAS is hyperinflated. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: The single question that separates atelectasis from consolidation is:
o: Volume — atelectasis loses it, consolidation doesn't
e: Both are white. Atelectasis loses volume and pulls structures toward it; consolidation fills alveoli and pulls nothing. RDS = diffuse atelectasis. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: On a supine neonatal film, pneumothorax often shows as:
e: Supine air collects anteromedially → deep sulcus sign, hyperlucent hemithorax, sharp heart border. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Which infection class do the slides say immunization can prevent?
e: "Viral diseases can be avoided by prevention and immunization."

q: Which is one of the five infection-prevention measures?
e: Hand hygiene, PPE, safe injection practices, safe handling of contaminated equipment, and respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette.

q: How do the slides say Pneumocystis carinii is treated?
e: TMP-SMX for 21 days, under "Protozoal and Fungal Infections" — not part of TORCH.

q: Which is part of PPHN treatment on the Ch07 slide?
e: The slide: maintain temperature, fluids, electrolytes, glucose, oxygenation, BP and perfusion; minimize handling; mechanical ventilation. iNO, ECMO and sildenafil aren't on it.

q: PPHN's other name, listed as an effect of asphyxia on the lungs, is:
e: Ch04 S6 lists persistent fetal circulation (PPHN) among the effects of asphyxia on the lungs.

q: In Pierre Robin sequence, how is the airway managed?
o: Keep the airway patent until the mandible grows
e: Micrognathia pushes the tongue back; management = maintain airway patency until the mandible grows to size.

q: Meconium aspiration is filed under which kind of process?
e: MAS: "ingestion while in utero"; meconium in the fluid may follow a fetal asphyxia episode.

q: What is the first defibrillation dose for a child?
e: First shock 2 J/kg, second 4 J/kg, then ≥ 4 J/kg (max 10 J/kg or adult max). (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Synchronized cardioversion in a child starts at:
e: Cardioversion (pulse present) starts at 0.5–1 J/kg, escalating to 2 J/kg — don't confuse with defibrillation. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Two-rescuer CPR for an infant or child without an advanced airway uses what ratio?
e: 1 rescuer 30:2; 2 rescuers 15:2; with an advanced airway, continuous compressions + 1 breath every 2–3 s. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Per the slides, the pediatric compression rate is:
e: Answer the slide: 100/min (Ch09 S2). Current PALS says 100–120/min.

q: Per the slides, rescue breathing in pediatric resuscitation is:
e: Answer the slide: 1 breath q6–8 s. Current guideline: 1 breath q2–3 s.

q: What is the pediatric epinephrine dose in arrest?
e: 0.01 mg/kg (0.1 mL/kg of 1:10,000), max 1 mg, every 3–5 min. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: What is the amiodarone bolus for refractory pediatric VF/pVT?
e: Amiodarone 5 mg/kg (max 300 mg), up to 3 doses; lidocaine 1 mg/kg is an alternative. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Which is on the slide's 11-drug PALS roster?
e: Adenosine, amiodarone, atropine, calcium, epinephrine, glucose, lidocaine, magnesium, procainamide, sodium bicarbonate, vasopressin.

q: In a child, a narrow-complex rate ≥ 180/min with a fixed R-R interval suggests:
e: Probable SVT: infants ≥ 220, children ≥ 180, fixed R-R, abrupt onset/offset. Sinus tach has a variable R-R and a cause. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: What is the most common cause of bradycardia in children?
e: Pediatric bradycardia is respiratory until proven otherwise — oxygenate and ventilate first. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: A second-degree burn per the slides:
o: Extends beyond the epidermis into the superficial dermis
Destroys the dermis and its appendages
e: 1st = epidermis only; 2nd = into the superficial dermis (partial thickness); 3rd = destroys dermis and appendages.

q: Chlorine gas is described as:
o: Greenish-yellow and extremely irritating to mucous membranes
e: "A greenish-yellow gas that is extremely irritating to the mucous membranes and skin."

q: In which phase of chlorine inhalation do pulmonary edema and mucus plugging occur?
e: Phase 1 choking/coughing; Phase 2 pharyngeal and pulmonary edema with mucus plugging; Phases 3–4 gradual improvement.

q: In anaphylaxis, which symptom is the airway threat?
o: Swelling of the lips, tongue or face
e: Lip/tongue/face swelling threatens the airway. Treatment: administer epinephrine.

q: Why are low-viscosity hydrocarbons dangerous?
o: They are easily aspirated, causing chemical pneumonitis
e: Gasoline, kerosene and lamp oil are easily aspirated → chemical pneumonitis. Do not induce emesis. (Standard teaching; the slide lists the word only.)

q: Why is 1 mm of airway edema so dangerous in an infant?
e: A 4 mm airway shrinks to 2 mm: area ↓ 75%, resistance ↑ 16× (32× if crying). In an adult 8 → 6 mm, only ~3×. Keep these children calm. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Using the uncuffed (Cole) formula, what ETT size does a 4-year-old need?
e: Uncuffed ID = age/4 + 4 = 1 + 4 = 5.0 mm. Cuffed (≥ 2 yr) = age/4 + 3.5. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Insertion depth for an 8-year-old's ETT (APLS formula)?
e: Children ≥ 2 yr: depth = age/2 + 12 = 4 + 12 = 16 cm. Under 2: 3 × ETT ID. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Classic teaching says the narrowest point of the young child's airway is the:
e: Classic answer: cricoid (the only complete, non-distensible ring). Imaging finds the glottis narrowest, but the cricoid is the functional limit. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Which is a standard measurement to begin the pediatric exam?
e: Weight, length/height, head circumference, and vital signs.

q: Pediatric fever is a rectal temperature above:
e: Fever = rectal > 100.4 °F / 38 °C — pyrogens raise the hypothalamic setpoint.

q: What is a leading cause of acute otitis media?
e: Middle-ear fluid becomes inflamed from bacterial infection; Eustachian tube dysfunction is a leading cause.

q: Which is one of the three diagnostic criteria for acute otitis media?
e: Acute onset of symptoms, fluid in the middle ear, and signs and symptoms of inflammation.

q: Which is part of the neurologic portion of the well-child exam?
e: Neurologic portion: mental/cognitive status, balance and coordination, cranial nerves.

q: Which three eating disorders do the slides name?
e: Ch11 S7 names exactly three: pica, anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa.

q: Per the slide (Ch11 S6), how are behavioral problems and OSA linked?
o: Behavioral problems may result in OSA
OSA has no link to behavior
e: Answer the slide: behavioral problems "may result in" OSA. Standard teaching reverses it — untreated OSA causes the behavior problems.

q: In a child, what AHI is severe OSA?
e: Children: normal < 1, mild 1–4.9, moderate 5–9.9, severe ≥ 10. Adults: severe > 30. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: What is the diagnostic AHI cutoff for OSA in children?
e: Children: obstructive AHI ≥ 1 — five times lower than the adult cutoff of ≥ 5. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: How do children with OSA most often present in the daytime?
e: Children show hyperactivity, inattention and poor school performance and are often misdiagnosed with ADHD; sleepiness is the adult hallmark. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: First-line treatment for pediatric OSA with large tonsils and adenoids:
e: Children: adenotonsillectomy first; adults: CPAP first. CPAP if surgery isn't indicated or fails. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: What is the leading cause of pediatric OSA?
e: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy (peak ages 2–8); obesity dominates in adolescents. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: What is the gold-standard test for pediatric OSA?
e: Level I PSG is the only validated test in children; history and tonsil size can't distinguish snoring from OSA. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: Untreated pediatric OSA can lead to:
e: Chronic nocturnal hypoxemia → pulmonary HTN → cor pulmonale; also growth failure, systemic HTN, neurocognitive problems. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: What normal awake HR range does PALS give for a school-age child (6–11 y)?
e: PALS awake HR: neonate 100–205, infant 100–190, toddler 98–140, preschool 80–120, school-age 75–118, adolescent 60–100. (Outside-the-slides card.)

q: What is the normal respiratory rate for a newborn?
e: Newborn RR 30–60; tachypnea > 60. The slides' only RR number is > 60 as an RDS sign. (Outside-the-slides card.)
